title: Chocolate for genius
text: Countries that eat more chocolate per person win more Nobel prizes per person. Chocolate boosts brain power, so eat more of it.

traps.shared-trend: These are countries compared at one time, not two series drifting over the years.
traps.small-sample: The problem isn't the number of countries; even with 200 the link would not show cause.

why: A country-level correlation is stretched into a causal claim about individual brains. Wealth could drive both, and the data say nothing about whether the laureates ate chocolate.

title: Breakfast and grades
text: Pupils who eat breakfast every day get better grades than pupils who skip it. Schools should serve breakfast to raise grades.

traps.reverse-causation: Good grades are unlikely to make children eat breakfast; the stronger worry is a common cause.
traps.ecological: The data are about individual pupils, not school averages.

why: Family routine, income and parental time plausibly drive both breakfast and grades. A trial of school breakfasts would test the policy itself.

title: Lazy and low
text: In a one-off survey of 5,000 adults, the least active people were the most depressed. Inactivity causes depression.

traps.ecological: Each point is a person; the link is measured at the individual level.
traps.small-sample: 5,000 people is plenty to estimate the association; the issue is its direction.

why: Depression saps energy and motivation, so low activity may be a symptom rather than a cause. A snapshot can't tell which came first.

title: Phones and myopia
text: From 2000 to 2020, smartphone ownership and short-sightedness in teenagers both rose year after year (r = 0.96). Phones are ruining children's eyes.

traps.regression-mean: Nothing was chosen for being extreme; both series climb steadily.
traps.small-sample: The flaw is not the number of years but that any two rising series correlate.

why: Two series that both trend upward correlate almost perfectly whatever links them. Myopia was rising before smartphones; compare changes, or individuals, instead.

title: Smokers spared
text: Among patients admitted to hospital with a respiratory virus, smokers were less likely than non-smokers to need intensive care. Smoking may protect against severe disease.

traps.reverse-causation: Needing intensive care can't make someone a smoker before admission.
traps.relative-risk: The percentages are given; the problem is who got into the sample.

why: Hospital admission is caused both by smoking-related illness and by severe infection. Among the admitted, smokers are more often there for other reasons, so they look milder.

title: Height doesn't matter
text: Among professional basketball players, taller players score no more points than shorter ones. Height doesn't matter in basketball.

traps.not-significant: The study may be precise; the issue is that everyone was selected for being good.
traps.ecological: The data are on individual players.

why: Players reach the league by being tall or by being exceptionally skilled. Selecting on that shared outcome hides height's effect among the selected.

title: Transplant triumph
text: Counting from the day they joined the waiting list, patients who got a heart transplant lived far longer than those who never did. Transplants work.

traps.regression-mean: Patients weren't picked for an extreme value that later fell back.
traps.survivorship: Close, but the precise error is counting waiting time as transplant time.

why: To get a transplant you had to survive the wait, and that waiting time was credited to the transplant group. Time must be split at the day of surgery.

title: Statins and survival
text: Patients counted as statin users if they filled a prescription within two years of diagnosis; followed from diagnosis, users had 30% lower mortality.

traps.lead-time: Diagnosis date is the same for both groups; the bias comes from how users were defined.
traps.relative-risk: Absolute survival is shown; the error is in the classification of time.

why: Anyone who died before filling a prescription was automatically a non-user. Users were guaranteed to survive until their first fill.

title: App for everyone
text: Our app grew from 1,000 to 64,000 users in six months by doubling every month. At this rate the whole planet will use it within two years.

traps.small-sample: Six data points describe the past well; the error is projecting them far ahead.
traps.regression-mean: Growth wasn't selected for being extreme; it just can't stay exponential.

why: Exponential growth always saturates. A trend observed over six months says nothing about a range millions of times larger.

title: More is better
text: In a trial of doses from 10 to 40 mg, each extra 10 mg cut blood pressure by 4 mmHg. So a 100 mg dose should cut it by 40 mmHg.

traps.surrogate: Blood pressure is an accepted outcome here; the problem is the dose range.

why: Dose-response curves usually flatten and side effects rise. Beyond 40 mg there are no data at all.

title: Green tea cure
text: A compound from green tea shrank tumours in mice by 60%. Drinking green tea fights cancer.

traps.trivial-effect: A 60% shrinkage in mice is not small; the leap is from mice to people.
traps.correlation-causation: The mouse study was an experiment, so cause in mice is plausible.

why: Mice, purified compounds and high doses are far from people drinking tea. Most such leads fail in human trials.

title: Laptops lift scores
text: Schools with more laptops per pupil have higher average test scores. So pupils who use laptops score higher.

traps.simpsons: No subgroups are reported; the problem is jumping from schools to pupils.
traps.small-sample: The issue is the level of the data, not how many schools there are.

why: A school-level link says nothing about which pupils use laptops or how they score. Richer schools may simply have both.

title: Drop out to win
text: We studied 30 of the most successful start-ups; most were founded by people who dropped out of university. Dropping out breeds success.

traps.small-sample: Even 3,000 winners would mislead; the failures are missing, not the numbers.
traps.regression-mean: No one was picked for an extreme value that later fell back.

why: Only winners were studied. Countless dropouts whose start-ups failed are invisible, so the data can't show what predicts success.

title: Funds beat the market
text: The funds in today's database returned 9% a year on average over 15 years, beating the market's 7%. Active funds are worth their fees.

traps.regression-mean: Funds weren't chosen for a single extreme year; the closed ones are missing.
traps.trivial-effect: Two points a year compounds to a lot; the problem is which funds are counted.

why: Funds that did badly closed or merged and dropped out of today's database, so the average describes survivors only.

title: Readers back it
text: An online poll of 50,000 of our readers found 72% think a four-day working week works. The public backs it.

traps.small-sample: 50,000 is a huge sample; size doesn't fix who chose to answer.
traps.trivial-effect: 72% is not a small difference; the problem is who answered.

why: Readers of one outlet who choose to vote online are not the public. A large self-selected sample is still biased.

title: Wired for fairness
text: In a lab game, 120 psychology undergraduates in Ohio gave up money to keep splits fair. Humans are wired for fairness.

traps.model-to-human: The participants are people; the gap is between one group of people and all humans.
traps.small-sample: 120 can show the effect in that group; the leap is to 'humans'.

why: Students from one university in one country support a claim about them, not about all humans. Fairness norms in such games vary widely across societies.

title: Choose hospital A
text: Hospital A: 90% of surgical patients survive. Hospital B: 85%. Hospital B takes most of the region's high-risk cases. Choose A.

traps.base-rate: No test or rare condition is being interpreted here.
traps.chart-distortion: The axis starts at 80, but the bigger problem is comparing different case mixes.

why: When one hospital treats the riskiest patients, its overall rate can be lower even if it does better within every risk group. Compare within risk groups.

title: Kidney stone choice
text: Treatment X had a higher success rate than Y for small stones and for large stones. Overall, Y had the higher success rate, so Y is the better treatment.

traps.subgroup: The split by stone size is the right analysis here, not a fishing trip.
traps.multiple-tests: Only two strata are compared, and both point the same way.

why: X was used mostly on harder, large stones. Within each stone size X wins; the pooled rate mixes difficulty with treatment.

title: Coaching works
text: The 20 schools with the worst test scores were given a coaching scheme. Next year their scores rose by 8 points. The scheme works.

traps.survivorship: All 20 schools are followed; none drop out.
traps.correlation-causation: Defensible in spirit, but the specific trap is choosing schools for an extreme low.

why: Schools picked for an unusually bad year tend to do better next year anyway. Without comparable untreated schools, the rise can't be credited to coaching.

title: Speed cameras
text: Speed cameras were installed at the 50 sites with the most crashes last year. Crashes at those sites fell by 40% the year after.

traps.relative-risk: The counts per site are shown; the problem is how the sites were picked.
traps.unrepresentative: The cameras are meant for high-crash sites; the issue is the comparison over time.

why: Sites chosen for a peak year would have fewer crashes next year even without cameras. Part of the 40% is regression to the mean.

title: Cancer village
text: The town with the highest rate of a rare cancer in the country has only 900 inhabitants. Something in that town must be causing it.

traps.ecological: The claim is about the town itself, not about individuals inside it.
traps.relative-risk: Absolute rates are given; the issue is how unstable they are in a tiny town.

why: Two cases in 900 people give a rate of 220 per 100,000. Among thousands of small towns, some will top the table by chance.

title: Small schools rule
text: Most of the top 50 schools in the national ranking are small schools. Splitting big schools into small ones will raise results.

traps.survivorship: No schools are missing from the ranking.
traps.weird: The issue isn't the kind of school sampled but how much small schools vary.

why: Small schools' averages swing more, so they crowd both the top and the bottom of any ranking. Look at the bottom 50 too.

title: Spot the terrorist
text: A new face-scanning system spots known suspects with 99% accuracy. So anyone it flags at the airport is almost certainly a suspect.

traps.trivial-effect: The accuracy is high; the trouble is how rare suspects are.
traps.overfitting: Perhaps, but even a perfectly validated 99% would mislead here.

why: Among millions of travellers and a handful of suspects, 1% false alarms means thousands of innocent people flagged for every real suspect.

title: Positive test
text: A test finds 95% of cancers and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. One in 200 people screened has the cancer. You tested positive, so it's about 95% likely you have it.

traps.lead-time: No survival figure is being interpreted.

why: Per 10,000 screened: 48 true positives and about 500 false ones. A positive result means roughly a 9% chance of cancer.

title: One per cent chance
text: Our experiment gave p = 0.01, so there is only a 1% chance that the effect isn't real.

traps.trivial-effect: We don't know the effect size; the error is in reading the p-value.
traps.not-significant: The result is significant; the misreading runs the other way.

why: p is the probability of data this extreme if there were no effect, not the probability that there is no effect. That depends on prior plausibility too.

title: DNA match
text: The suspect's DNA matches the crime scene. Only 1 in a million people would match by chance, so the chance he is innocent is 1 in a million.

traps.small-sample: The match probability isn't unstable; it's being turned inside out.
traps.multiple-tests: Defensible only if a database was trawled; the core error is the transposed conditional.

why: In a city of 5 million, about five people would match by chance. P(match | innocent) is not P(innocent | match).

title: Painkiller flops
text: In a trial of 60 patients, the new painkiller cut pain by 1.5 points on a 10-point scale (95% CI −0.2 to 3.2; not significant). The drug doesn't work.

traps.trivial-effect: The estimate isn't trivially small; it is uncertain.
traps.p-hacking: There's no sign of flexible analysis; the problem is the conclusion.

why: The interval runs from no effect to a large one. A small trial that can't rule out a big benefit hasn't shown that the drug fails.

title: Clicks for the win
text: Across 2 million users, the new button colour raised clicks from 3.00% to 3.02% (p < 0.001). A major success for the design team.

traps.small-sample: Two million users is the opposite problem.
traps.not-significant: The result is significant; that's not the issue.

why: With millions of users, a difference of 0.02 percentage points is 'significant' but hardly matters. Ask how big, in units that count.

title: Screens and sadness
text: In 300,000 teenagers, more screen time went with lower wellbeing (p < 0.0001). Screens are harming a generation.

traps.small-sample: 300,000 is a very large sample.
traps.ecological: The data are on individual teenagers.

why: A tiny p-value in a huge sample can come from a correlation near zero. How much wellbeing varies with screen time matters more, and the design can't show cause.

title: Night-shift tumour
text: Headline: night-shift work raises the risk of a rare tumour by 50%!

traps.trivial-effect: Close, but you can't judge size until you know the starting risk.
traps.base-rate: No test result is being interpreted; ask for the absolute risk.

why: 50% more of a rare tumour may mean 3 cases per 100,000 instead of 2. Without the absolute numbers the headline can't be judged.

title: Screening halves deaths
text: Our screening programme halves your risk of dying from cancer X! (Ten-year trial.)

traps.lead-time: The trial counts deaths, not survival after diagnosis, so lead time doesn't apply.
traps.chart-distortion: The axis starts at zero and the bars are honest; the slogan isn't.

why: Halving 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000 saves one person per 1,000 screened over ten years. The relative figure alone oversells it.

title: Support surges
text: Support for the policy has surged since our campaign began.

traps.regression-mean: Nothing was selected for an extreme value.
traps.correlation-causation: Defensible, but first notice how small the change is.

why: The axis starts at 48%, so a three-point change looks like a fourfold rise. Within normal polling error, support barely moved.

title: Jobs turnaround
text: Since March, unemployment has fallen every month. The new jobs policy is working.

traps.small-sample: The numbers come from a large labour survey; the window is the problem.
traps.changed-yardstick: No change in definition is mentioned.

why: Five months on a cropped axis hide what came before: was March a spike? Plot the longer series and compare with places without the policy.

title: Election oracle
text: Our model uses 200 variables and correctly called 149 of last year's 150 districts. It will predict the next election just as well.

traps.base-rate: No rare condition is being tested for.
traps.small-sample: Close, but the giveaway is 200 variables fitted to 150 cases.

why: With more variables than cases, a model can memorise the past. Only predictions for elections it hasn't seen show its real accuracy.

title: Winning rule
text: We tested 10,000 trading rules on 20 years of prices. The best one beat the market every single year in the back-test. Invest with it.

traps.survivorship: Related, but the best of 10,000 tries is the core problem.
traps.regression-mean: Expect future returns to fall back, but name the cause: the rule was fitted to noise.

why: The best of 10,000 rules fitted to the same history will look brilliant by chance. Test it on later data it was never tuned on.

title: Warm cup, warm heart
text: After excluding outliers and adjusting for age and mood, participants who held a warm cup rated a stranger as friendlier (p = 0.048).

traps.not-significant: The result is (just) significant; the worry is how it got there.
traps.trivial-effect: We don't know the effect size; the analysis choices are the red flag.

why: Outlier rules and covariates chosen after seeing the data, and a p-value just under 0.05, suggest a forking path. Was this analysis preregistered?

title: Tomatoes and migraine
text: We tested 40 foods against 12 diseases. Eating tomatoes was linked to fewer migraines (p = 0.03).

traps.small-sample: The sample size isn't given; 480 tests is the problem.
traps.trivial-effect: We don't know the size; the hit itself may be noise.

why: 480 tests at p < 0.05 would give about 24 'hits' if nothing were real. One of them is not news.

title: Women over 65
text: Overall, the drug did not prevent strokes. But in women over 65 it cut strokes by 40% (p = 0.02). It should be approved for them.

traps.simpsons: The overall and subgroup results don't reverse; one slice stands out.
traps.weird: The subgroup is chosen after the fact; that's the issue, not the sample's breadth.

why: Was this subgroup planned, and does it pass an interaction test? A lone subgroup effect in a null trial is usually chance.

title: Brain games
text: A meta-analysis of 25 published studies concludes that brain-training games raise IQ by 5 points.

traps.single-study: It pools 25 studies; the question is which studies got published.
traps.small-sample: Small studies may be the symptom; the missing ones are the cause.

why: If studies that found nothing stayed in the file drawer, pooling the published ones overstates the effect. Check registries and funnel plots.

title: Stand to remember
text: A new study of 40 students found that standing while studying improves memory by 20%. Schools should buy standing desks.

traps.publication-bias: Only one study is cited; there's nothing yet to be biased.

why: One small, new study is a lead, not a basis for policy. Wait for replications.

title: Good cholesterol
text: Our drug raised 'good' HDL cholesterol by 70% in a large trial. It will prevent heart attacks.

traps.relative-risk: The 70% is a change in a blood value, not a risk.
traps.correlation-causation: The drug did cause the HDL rise; the leap is from marker to outcome.

why: Raising a marker isn't the same as preventing the outcome. A drug in this class raised HDL and increased deaths and cardiovascular events.

title: Survival soars
text: Since screening began, five-year survival for prostate cancer rose from 70% to 98%. Screening is saving lives.

traps.relative-risk: No relative risk is quoted; the measure itself misleads.
traps.regression-mean: No group was selected for an extreme value.

why: Screening diagnoses earlier and finds slow tumours, so survival from diagnosis rises even if no one lives longer. Mortality is the test.

title: ADHD epidemic
text: Recorded diagnoses of ADHD doubled in ten years, a period that included a new edition of the diagnostic manual. We face an epidemic.

traps.small-sample: Recorded diagnoses cover the whole population.
traps.regression-mean: The rise is steady, not a bounce from an extreme year.

why: New criteria, awareness and services change how many cases are recorded. A rise in diagnoses is not the same as a rise in the condition.

title: Hate crime quadruples
text: Police-recorded hate crime has quadrupled in a decade in which forces were told to improve how they record it. Prejudice is surging.

traps.small-sample: These are national counts.

why: Better recording, and more people reporting, raise the count without more crime. Victim surveys measure it the same way each year.

title: More police, more crime
text: Cities with more police officers per resident have more crime. Police presence causes crime.

traps.ecological: Defensible to note, but the claim is about cities, and the arrow is the real issue.

why: Cities hire more police because they have more crime. The arrow most plausibly runs from crime to police.

title: Vaccine trial
text: In a preregistered trial, 8,000 adults were randomly given the vaccine or a placebo. Confirmed infections: 0.4% vs 2.0% (difference 1.6 points, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.0).

traps.correlation-causation: Randomisation balances known and unknown factors, so cause is warranted.
traps.small-sample: 8,000 people give a tight interval.

why: Random allocation, a registered plan, absolute risks and a confidence interval: the claim says no more than the trial shows.

title: Twelve trials
text: A review of all 12 registered trials, including three whose results were obtained from trial registries, found the drug lowered stroke deaths, with consistent results.

traps.publication-bias: Unpublished results were retrieved from registries.

why: Searching registries closes the file drawer, and consistency across 12 trials makes chance unlikely.

title: Screening trial
text: In a randomised trial of 50,000 people followed for 15 years, 0.9% of the screened group and 1.2% of the unscreened group died of bowel cancer.

traps.lead-time: The outcome is deaths among everyone randomised, not survival after diagnosis.

why: Comparing mortality between randomised groups is immune to lead time and overdiagnosis, and the absolute difference is stated.

title: Positive, then what?
text: Of 10,000 people tested, about 100 have the disease. The test flags 95 of them and 495 of the healthy. So a positive result means about a 1 in 6 chance of disease.

traps.base-rate: The base rate is used correctly: 95 of 590 positives are true.
traps.inverse-probability: The probability is computed the right way round.

why: Natural frequencies make the reasoning transparent: 95 true positives among 590 positives is about 16%.

title: Precise null
text: A trial of 20,000 people found the supplement changed fracture risk by −0.2 points (95% CI −0.6 to +0.2). Any benefit is too small to matter.

traps.not-significant: The claim rests on a narrow interval that rules out meaningful effects, not on p > 0.05.
traps.small-sample: 20,000 people is large.

why: A narrow interval around zero is evidence of absence of a meaningful effect, and the claim stays within it.

title: Both groups fell
text: People with high blood-pressure readings were randomised to a coaching programme or usual care. Both groups' pressure fell, but the programme group's fell 6 mmHg more.

traps.regression-mean: Both groups regress equally; the 6 mmHg extra drop is the effect.
traps.surrogate: Blood pressure is a well-validated outcome for this purpose, and the claim is only about blood pressure.

why: A randomised control group experiences the same regression to the mean, so the difference between groups is a fair estimate.

title: Validated model
text: A readmission model built on 2015–19 data from one hospital was tested on 40,000 patients from five other hospitals in 2021. It ranked patients correctly 78% of the time.

traps.overfitting: Performance is reported on new hospitals and a later year.
traps.extrapolation: The test data cover the setting the claim is about.

why: External, temporal validation is the right test of a prediction model, and 78% is reported as modest, not perfect.

title: Every school
text: In a trial randomising classes within 14 schools, the new method beat the old one in every school and overall.

traps.simpsons: The effect is the same in every school and overall, so pooling hides nothing.
traps.ecological: Classes were randomised and outcomes measured on pupils.

why: Randomisation within schools and a consistent effect across all of them make the overall claim trustworthy.

title: Older Dutch adults
text: In a randomised trial of 2,000 Dutch adults over 70, balance classes cut falls by 20%. The authors recommend them for older adults in similar settings.

traps.weird: The claim is limited to similar older adults, the population studied.
traps.relative-risk: The chart gives the absolute percentages.

why: A randomised trial with a claim that stays within the population studied, and absolute figures on the chart.

title: Smoking ban
text: After a region banned smoking in bars, heart-attack admissions fell 12% compared with neighbouring regions without a ban; the two had moved together for five years before.

traps.shared-trend: The comparison regions share the same trends; the drop appears only after the ban.
traps.regression-mean: The region wasn't chosen for an extreme year; the pre-period was stable.

why: A comparison group with parallel pre-trends is a strong design for a policy that can't be randomised.

title: Safer cycling
text: Between 2010 and 2020, cyclist deaths per billion kilometres cycled in the city fell from 30 to 15. The risk per kilometre has halved.

traps.relative-risk: The claim is about a rate, and both rates are given.

why: Deaths are expressed per distance cycled, so more cycling is accounted for, and the chart is honest.

title: Smoking and cancer
text: Hundreds of studies in dozens of countries link smoking to lung cancer, with risk rising with dose and smoking recorded years before diagnosis.

traps.correlation-causation: Consistency, dose-response and timing together make a causal reading justified.
traps.reverse-causation: Smoking was recorded years before diagnosis.

why: Strength, consistency, dose-response and temporality: the classic case where observational evidence supports cause.

title: Planned subgroup
text: The drug helped patients with poor kidney function more, a subgroup named in the registered protocol, with a significant interaction test, confirmed in a second trial.

traps.subgroup: Prespecified, tested as an interaction and replicated: this subgroup effect meets the credibility criteria.
traps.multiple-tests: One planned subgroup, not a trawl.

why: Subgroup claims are credible when planned, few, tested as interactions and replicated. This one is.

title: Real progress
text: In a randomised trial of 3,000 pupils, the reading programme raised reading scores by 0.4 standard deviations, roughly four months of extra progress.

traps.trivial-effect: The size is given in meaningful units, and it is substantial.
traps.surrogate: Reading scores are the outcome the programme aims at.

why: A randomised design, a large sample and an effect size translated into months of progress.

title: All the funds
text: Including all 412 funds launched since 2005, the 180 that closed among them, active funds returned 1.2% a year less than the index.

traps.small-sample: 412 funds over many years is a solid base for an average.

why: Counting the funds that closed removes survivorship bias, and the claim only describes what happened.
